```{python}
#| echo: false
from pbc.authoring import lesson_header
from pbc.mechanics.experiments import scientific_review as experiment

result = experiment.run()
lesson_header()
```

A piece of simulation code is handed over with a sentence about what it does:
here, that it is a first-order method for Newton's second law and that the
energy of an oscillator it steps stays in a band. Someone has to decide
whether to believe the sentence. The lesson on verifying scientific code gave
that someone five checks. This lesson gives the checks to language models,
three of them, with different jobs, and keeps the one thing a model should not
be trusted with out of their hands: the verdict.

Each reviewer is one run of the loop of the first agent lesson. One looks at
the physics, one at the numerical implementation, one at the evidence. Each
has its own short list of tools, and each tool runs a check of the contract on
one of two pieces of code. One piece is the symplectic Euler stepper of the
course. The other is a variant with a fault that a reader could miss. The
reviewers do not know which is which, and they do not see each other's work.

What the page shows is what the build recomputed. The reviewers' words are a
recording; every check they asked for is run again, and the verdicts below come
from those runs.

## Assumptions

1. **The claim comes first.** Both pieces claim first order and a bounded
   energy of the oscillator. A reviewer is asked whether the code does what it
   claims, and a claim written after the checks would be a description.
2. **The checks are the contract's, and they are shared.** The three
   reviewers use the same functions with the same tolerances, fixed before any
   piece was run. They differ in which checks they may run, not in what a
   check means. If they could choose their own tolerances, a disagreement
   might only be a disagreement about tolerances.
3. **A reviewer's words are data.** A model may write that code passes when
   it does not, or the reverse. The verdict of this page is read from the
   results of the tools, never from the text.
4. **A pass covers what was run.** A reviewer that ran three checks says
   nothing about the other two. Where reviewers differ, the cause is usually
   that they ran different checks, and the resolution rule is written for
   that case.
5. **The oscillator is a fair reference, and only one.** A fault that matters
   for a force that depends on the velocity could pass every check here. The
   contract says what to add for a new model, and the evidence reviewer is
   asked to say what its evidence does not cover.
6. **A recording is a record.** It shows what one model once did with this
   task. The numbers in it are checked; the reasoning is not.

## Three jobs, one rule {#explanation}

The reviewers are three runs of the same loop with different system prompts
and different allowlists:

- the **physics** reviewer may run the checks `limits` and `bounded-energy`:
  does the code reproduce the motions with a closed form, and does it keep the
  quantity it says it conserves;
- the **numerics** reviewer may run `clock`, `purity`, and
  `convergence-order`: does a step behave as a step of a method of the claimed
  order must;
- the **evidence** reviewer may reproduce any of the five checks in the order
  of the contract, and may ask for the raw error against the exact oscillator
  at a number of time steps, so that it can write the evidence in the contract's
  form, with the name of the check and the call from its own calls, and say what is not covered.

There is no new machinery. The boundary of the first agent lesson holds
unchanged: a model can only name a tool of its list and give numbers within
bounds, the loop stops after a fixed number of messages, and the harness has
no code that evaluates what a model writes. A reviewer has even less to
ask for than the experimenter of the first lesson: its tools take the number of
a piece of code, 1 or 2, and the number of a check.

### Disagreement and resolution

The three runs are compared by the build, not by a fourth model. Each tool
result carries the numbers of a finding in the contract's form (rule 3): the
measured value, the tolerance, and whether it passed. The name of the check and
the call that reproduces it are in the reviewer's own tool call, and the claim
is the one both pieces make; the build recomputes the numbers, not these. The rule that combines them is one sentence:

> A check that failed when it was recomputed stands, whatever the other
> reviewers said. A reviewer that did not run that check has no standing
> against it.

So a disagreement is not settled by a vote. When two reviewers recompute the
same check, they get the same number, because the check is deterministic; if
they did not, the build reports a conflict. When one reviewer found a failure
and another did not, the second ran other checks, and the list of what each
ran says which.

## Worked examples

### The two pieces of code

Piece 1 is the stepper of the course. Piece 2 is a variant that looks like it:
it moves the particle with the old velocity, so the two updates are in the
wrong order. Both claim the order and the bounded energy of
`{python} result["claim"]`.

```{python}

from pbc.mechanics.integrators import symplectic_euler_step
from pbc.verification.faulty import explicit_euler_as_symplectic

excerpt(symplectic_euler_step)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false

```

The second function is wrong on purpose: it is in the gallery of faulty
steppers of the earlier lesson, the only module outside the lessons and tests
that imports it is the one that sets up this review.

### Where they agree, and where they do not

This is the part of the page that is decided. Every line is built from the
recomputed results of the tools, and no text of a reviewer is in it.

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.display("review")
```

The numerics reviewer ran three checks and passed both pieces, and was right
about what it ran: the faulty piece has the correct order, a correct clock,
and no hidden state. It did not run `bounded-energy`. The physics reviewer
and the evidence reviewer did, and the recomputed check failed for piece 2.
By the rule, the failure stands.

That is the reason to want several reviewers, and the reason not to count
them. Had the numerics reviewer been the only one, the review would have passed a
method whose energy grows by a factor of `{python} result["growth"]` over a
hundred periods.

### A reviewer cannot talk its way past the build

The recorded reviewers wrote honest summaries. A model need not. The cell below
plays a reviewer that calls the check on piece 2 and then says the piece
passes every check; the verdict is read from the result of the call.

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.Boaster)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.boasting_reviewer)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
print(result.output("boasting-reviewer"), end="")
```

### The replay keeps the page honest

The replay compares every recomputed result with the recorded one, to a
relative and absolute difference of `{python} result["tolerance"]`. If a check
of the contract changes, a recording is no longer a recording of what the code
does. Here the tolerance of the exact checks is made tighter than round-off,
and the physics reviewer is replayed.

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.stricter_check)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
print(result.output("stricter-check"), end="")
```

The build would fail with that message. The maintainer then runs the reviewers
live, reads the new runs, and commits the new recordings.

### What the evidence reviewer saw

The evidence reviewer asked for the error against the exact oscillator at
three step counts. The figure shows what the build recomputed, with a fresh
scan of the same two pieces.

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.draw_review_evidence)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-review-evidence
#| echo: false
#| fig-status: simulated
#| fig-cap: "Error against the exact oscillator over two periods, against the number of time steps per period, for pieces 1 and 2. Lines are a fresh scan; dots are the values the evidence reviewer asked for, recomputed by this build."
#| fig-alt: "A log-log chart of error against steps per period, from 20 to 800. Two lines fall with a slope close to minus one; the line of piece 2 lies above that of piece 1. Dots mark 50, 100 and 200 steps for each piece, on the lines."
result.show("fig-review-evidence")
```

Both lines fall with a slope near $-1$: both are first-order methods, which is
why the order check passes both. The line of piece 2 sits higher, and the
figure does not show the thing that is wrong with it: an energy that grows
without bound. A convergence plot shows how fast the error falls at a fixed
time, and the energy test shows what happens to a long run. The contract has
both for that reason.

### Run the reviewers yourself

This needs your own key and costs a few cents. The build does not run it, so
the commands are marked.

::: {.not-verified}
```bash
# once: install the optional provider package
uv sync --extra openai

# in this shell only: the key stays out of code and files
export OPENAI_API_KEY="..."

uv run --extra openai python -m pbc.agents.review_lab
```
:::

It runs the three reviewers one after the other and prints each message and
tool call. A live run will differ in its words and perhaps in the order of its
calls; the numbers of the checks it asks for are the numbers on this page, and
the verdicts follow from them. The maintainer records the fixtures of this page
with `--record`, reads the files, and commits them.

## Exercises

::: {.exercise}
Run all five checks of the contract on both pieces yourself, without a reviewer.
Which check fails, and which of the three reviewers could have found it
with its own list of tools?

::: {.solution}
```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.every_check)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
print(result.output("every-check"), end="")
```

Only `bounded-energy` fails, for piece 2. The physics reviewer has it in its
list, and so has the evidence reviewer. The numerics reviewer does not, so its
review, however careful, could not have failed the piece. Which reviewer is
given which checks is part of the design of a review, and it should be written
down before the reviewers run.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
Two reviewers recompute the same check on the same piece and report different
verdicts. Build the verdicts by hand, resolve them, and say what the build
reports and what it means.

::: {.solution}
```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.a_conflict)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
print(result.output("a-conflict"), end="")
```

The failed check stands, so the piece is rejected, and the check is reported as
a conflict. The checks are deterministic, so two honest reviewers get the same
number from the same check on the same code. A conflict means they did not
run the same check or the same code, and it is the reviewers' set-up that has
to be looked at before anything is concluded about the piece.
:::
:::
